summary: Implemented the T26 published prekey pool in PRODUCT CODE ONLY: `relay publish` now means "bring my published pool back up to N = LIMITS.PREKEY_MIN_COUNT", idempotent-with-top-up, through the unchanged publish route. Four files changed, all under apps/cli/src - profile.ts (pool slots, publicationPool/restorePublicationPool/replacePublicationSlot, slot 0 still writing cli:publication unchanged), outbound.ts (publish() becomes the top-up loop), relayClient.ts (BUNDLE_EXPIRED added to the transport allowlist, the one thing T26's file list missed) and cli.ts (a false rationale comment). No test file was created, edited or deleted; all twelve relevant test files are shown byte-identical by SHA-256. No relay file, schema, wire field, route, config variable, rollout flag, ninth command or new option. Nothing was deployed and neither geekom nor depr was contacted. Eighteen of the nineteen target tests pass, including the e2e that is the whole point of the task: twenty distinct senders delivered from one pool, the recipient decrypted all twenty in one poll, the twenty-first was refused at exit 3 under PREKEY_BUNDLE_UNAVAILABLE, one `relay publish` restored the pool, and that same sender's own retry delivered. The nineteenth fails on ONE assertion that is arithmetically inconsistent with an assertion earlier in its own file, and a pre-existing publish-count assertion in two-process.test.ts that neither T29's F-001 nor T30 enumerated also fails. Both are test-file corrections and this dispatch forbids editing tests, so they are reported rather than made. Go: all packages ok with -count=1 and -race, tagged and untagged, ZERO data races; the permanent-reservation guards are untouched by digest and green.

acceptance.criterion: `relay publish` tops up rather than replacing: every stored member is re-submitted, and exactly one fresh member is minted per slot the relay will no longer serve
acceptance.evidence: outbound.publicationPool.test.ts tests 6-9 pass. Full pool: N requests, minted 0, every request body byte-identical to the stored member. Partial drain of 3: all N originals re-submitted INCLUDING the ones last seen as live, exactly 3 minted, each carrying a key id never offered before. Expired member: replaced silently, command succeeds, pool.minted counts it, no PROTOCOL_REJECTED reaches classify(). Anchor: bundleId unchanged across a full-pool publish, a partial-drain publish and an expired-member publish. The ordering decision that makes the anchor hold is recorded in the report: empty slots are filled from the highest index DOWN, so slot 0 carries the youngest created_at_ms and is the last member a claim reaches, because the relay serves the oldest available member first.

Twenty distinct published first-contact senders each delivered; the recipient polled once and got received === 20 with rejected === []; the twenty-first was refused at exit 3 under PREKEY_BUNDLE_UNAVAILABLE and explicitly not PROTOCOL_REJECTED; ONE `relay publish` reported minted === 20 and claimable === 20; that same sender re-ran the identical send with the identical --message-id and it delivered; and the following publish reported minted === 1, pinning that her retry consumed exactly one member.

findings.problem: `expect(drained).toBe(LIMITS.PREKEY_MIN_COUNT - 2)` is arithmetically inconsistent with step 6 of the same test, and no implementation of a pool top-up can satisfy both. Step 6 asserts pool.minted === 1 and pool.claimable === LIMITS.PREKEY_MIN_COUNT after alice's single claim - i.e. the top-up allocated a replacement and the pool is back at N = 20 LIVE members. Step 7 then has carol consume exactly one of those twenty. So nineteen remain for step 8's raw claims, and the loop drains nineteen before the relay refuses. The comment above the assertion - "Alice and carol consumed one member each, so exactly N-2 remain" - counts the two claims and forgets its own step 6 top-up.
findings.impact: This is the one of the nineteen target tests that does not pass, and its failure looks like an implementation defect while being a test defect. The trap for the next implementer is worse than the failure: the only ways to make 18 true are to stop minting a replacement for a consumed member (which contradicts step 6's own minted === 1, e2e prekey-pool-replenishment's minted === 20 after a total drain, and outbound.publicationPool.test.ts B-7's minted === 3) or to redefine pool.claimable as something other than live-members-after-top-up (which makes B-7's claimable === 20 after three members were consumed false instead). Either would ship a pool that under-restores, in the command that exists specifically to restore.
findings.suggested_fix: One value: `expect(drained).toBe(LIMITS.PREKEY_MIN_COUNT - 1)`, with the comment corrected to "alice and carol consumed one member each and the step-6 top-up replaced alice's, so exactly N-1 remain". Nothing else in the file changes - steps 1 through 7, including step 6's anchor-stability assertion and step 7's delivery inversion, all pass against this implementation. Note that line 271's `expect(exhausted).toEqual({status: 404, code: "PREKEY_BUNDLE_UNAVAILABLE"})` was never evaluated because 270 threw first; the loop did terminate on a relay refusal after 19 successful claims, but that status and code remain unmeasured and should be confirmed by the run that fixes 270.
findings.evidence: Measured twice, deterministically: in the full CLI suite (`npx vitest run`, 496 s) and in isolation (`npx vitest run test/e2e/publication-claimability.test.ts test/e2e/prekey-pool-replenishment.test.ts`, where the sibling e2e passed in 98.4 s). Both report `AssertionError: expected 19 to be 18` at publication-claimability.test.ts:270. The relay's availability scan takes the oldest unclaimed member first (storage/repository/signal_prekey_bundle_v2.go:86 writes the key `v2:available:<identity>:<created_at_ms as 16 digits>:<bundle_id>` and :155 scans that prefix ascending), so the count is not order-dependent: it is 20 minus the two claims plus the one replacement.

class_scope.enumeration_method: The class is assertions that compute how many pool members remain claimable on the relay after a mix of claims and top-ups. `keryx ctx rg 'PREKEY_MIN_COUNT [-+]'` over apps/ returns exactly three hits: this line, publication-claimability.test.ts:256 (`< LIMITS.PREKEY_MIN_COUNT + 2`, the raw-claim loop's liveness bound, which is not a residual count and is satisfied either way) and outbound.publish.test.ts:95 (a comment). Every other member-count assertion in the tree compares against LIMITS.PREKEY_MIN_COUNT itself or against a count of consumed slots derived inside the test, and all of those pass. A single-entry list is the claim here: this is the only site that derives a residual pool size by subtracting claims without accounting for the replacements the same test asserts were minted.

findings.problem: A seventh pre-existing publish-count assertion that neither T29's finding F-001 nor T30's corrections enumerated: `expect(traffic.filter((entry) => entry.path === "/v2/prekeys/publish" && entry.status === 200)).toHaveLength(2)`. F-001's enumeration searched for exact request-path array literals (`toEqual(["/v1...`) and for toHaveLength on a recorded attempts/requests array; this site expresses the same count through a filter over a proxy traffic log and matched neither pattern.

findings.problem: The pool moved these suites' per-child timing margin. `relay publish` on a fresh profile now mints twenty bundles at roughly 60 ms each, so a child that used to finish in well under a second now spends about 1.3 s minting before it makes its first request. Both cli.relayErrorCodes.test.ts and cli.senderQuota.test.ts spawn that child under a 15 000 ms SIGKILL of their own, and both hit it in the full-suite run, reporting `code: null, errorCode: "no-output"`.
findings.impact: Not a regression - both pass in isolation, which is the CPU-contention class the dispatch names - but the headroom is smaller than it was and a future flake in either suite will look like a protocol failure rather than a timeout. `errorCode: "no-output"` is a particularly misleading shape for a SIGKILL: it reads as a CLI that printed nothing, not as a child that was killed.
findings.suggested_fix: Nothing needs changing today. If either suite flakes again, raise its per-child budget rather than reaching for the runtime: 15 000 ms was chosen when `relay publish` was one request, and the same argument that produced vitest.config.ts's 30 000 ms testTimeout (T42-F-001: ~3x the worst observed loaded duration) now points at a larger number here. Separately, the two run helpers could distinguish a killed child from a silent one, so a timeout stops presenting as "no-output".

findings.problem: A deliberate divergence from T26 §2.7's sentence "`relay publish` fails only if *nothing* ends up claimable". This implementation absorbs only BUNDLE_EXPIRED as a dead slot; every other refusal - of a stored member or of a replacement's publish - propagates immediately, so a publish that had already restored nineteen members still fails if the twentieth is refused.
findings.impact: Strictly stricter than the design, never looser, and no test distinguishes the two readings (B-10 passes either way). The cost is that a single transient refusal mid-pool aborts a command that had done most of its work; the benefit is that a malformed or mis-signed member cannot be re-minted in silence forever, hiding a real defect behind an endless supply of fresh key material. Every slot already stored is durable, so the retry is idempotent and resumes rather than restarting.
findings.suggested_fix: Leave as implemented unless an operator meets it in practice. If §2.7's exact reading is wanted, the change is to collect replacement-publish failures instead of throwing and to raise only when claimable === 0 - but that trades a loud failure for a quiet partial success in the one command whose entire purpose is telling the operator what it restored, so it should be a decision rather than a tidy-up.
findings.evidence: outbound.ts publish(): the re-submission loop rethrows anything for which expiredPublication(error) is false, and the replacement loop does not catch at all. outbound.publicationPool.test.ts test 10 ("fails rather than reporting success when nothing at all ends up claimable") passes: with every member consumed and every fresh publication refused 409 BUNDLE_ID_CONFLICT, publish() rejects. outbound.publish.test.ts test 1 also depends on the fail-fast shape - `expect(lost.attempts).toHaveLength(1)` requires the very first refused request to end the command - and passes.

findings.problem: T26 §2.3's per-invocation request counts are low, as T29's F-004 predicted. `relay publish` issues 2N - k requests, not N: N re-submissions plus one publish per replaced slot. A full-drain top-up is 40 requests, not 20.
findings.impact: Against the shipped 120/min limiter a full-drain top-up is a third of the minute budget rather than the sixth §2.3 states, so three of them in a minute hit the limiter, not six. Nothing about the design changes; the number an operator is told does. The two figures that ARE exact: a first publish on an empty profile is N = 20 requests, and a steady-state publish on an untouched pool is N = 20.
findings.suggested_fix: Read §2.3's figures as "N mint-and-publish operations" and add the N re-submissions when quoting a per-invocation request count, in any document that repeats them. Measured wall-clock for a first publish on an unloaded host: about 1.2 s of minting, matching §1.2's 57.7 ms per bundle.
